implementation_notes: Scala 3's export clause is the language's answer to 'composition over inheritance': `export inner.{save, load}` creates class members that alias the delegate's members exactly as if forwarders had been written, with selectors for renaming (`as`), omission (`as _`) and given instances. The standard library's own justification is that object-oriented languages made inheritance cheap (`extends`) and composition expensive (a verbose sequence of forwarders), and that exports redress the balance. Exported term aliases are `final` and cannot override concrete members of a base class, which is the price of the brevity; Scala 2 code has no export and either writes the forwarders or uses `abstract override` stackable traits.
pitfalls: Export aliases are `final` and cannot override concrete members of a base class, so a class that extends a concrete class cannot use `export` to override its members - the facade must extend a trait or stand alone.
The exported member set is fixed at compile time: later additions to the delegate are not exported, and a simple selector that matches no eligible member is a compile error.

Type members are exported as type aliases and given instances only through a `given` selector, so an incomplete selector list (for example missing `given`) leaves implicit resolution silently unchanged.

variants.name: Scala 2 hand-written forwarders
variants.implementation_notes: Before Scala 3, composition over inheritance had to be written out: the wrapper extends the same trait and every member is a one-line forwarder (`def save(id: String): Unit = inner.save(id)`), or, when the delegate is itself a trait implementation, an `abstract override` layer can be mixed in to add behaviour around it. Scala 2 has no export clause and no compiler-generated forwarding, so the wrapper is maintained by hand unless a macro or code generator is used. Choose Scala 3's export when the toolchain allows it; keep this form for Scala 2 libraries that must compile on 2.13.
pitfalls: Forwarders are not checked for completeness against the trait's concrete members: an unimplemented abstract member is a compile error, but a concrete trait member is simply not delegated and the wrapper silently keeps the trait's default.
`abstract override` composes linearly in mixin order and requires every layer to declare the member the same way; a wrong order changes behaviour without a compile error.
Renaming a delegate member breaks only the forwarders that reference it - the wrapper's own signature stays valid, so callers keep compiling against a wrapper that now forwards less than they expect.
